name: domain-factory
intent: Shift responsibility for creating and reconstituting domain objects and aggregates to a dedicated creation owner, so clients obtain complete, invariant-respecting objects without knowing concrete classes or assembly steps.
problem: Creation logic is spread across call sites: every caller must know which inputs are mandatory, in which order sub-objects are assembled and which business rules must hold before an object exists, and the constructor either accepts unvalidated raw data or forces each caller to pre-validate. Rebuilding an object from a persistence row or an external payload is a second, differently constrained path, so creation knowledge gets duplicated and invalid objects reach the model.
context: Applies wherever a domain model has non-trivial construction: objects whose invariants must hold from birth, multi-step assembly, identity assignment, several input shapes (commands, rows, external messages) or polymorphic products behind a base type. It matters most in layered or hexagonal designs, where the domain must not depend on the persistence or transport formats it is rebuilt from, and where creation may need other aggregates, policies or id generators.
benefits: Construction knowledge has one owner: validation order, mandatory inputs, identity assignment and assembly steps live in the factory instead of at every call site.
Clients receive guaranteed-valid objects: with the product's constructor private to the factory, an instance that exists is an instance whose invariants were checked.
Call sites are decoupled from concrete classes and from assembly order; the factory can return a subtype or hide an entire object graph.
Raw-data translation becomes an explicit, testable boundary: a factory that maps rows, documents or external payloads to domain objects can be exercised without persistence or transport.
New creation paths are additive: a new named method or registered creator covers a new input shape without touching existing callers.
Creation reads in the ubiquitous language (Order.from_cart, Account.open_business, Payment.record_from_gateway) where a positional constructor would be cryptic.

Creation and reconstitution are separate entry points, each enforcing its own contract: new objects fail-fast on invariant violations and receive new identity; reconstituted objects receive existing identity and may require structural repair rather than rejection.

Creation can be modeled as a domain concept: an aggregate root creating another aggregate (e.g., ShoppingCart.createOrder) places the factory method in the ubiquitous language rather than in infrastructure.
tradeoffs: Indirection for its own sake: an object without invariants and with a plain argument list needs no factory - a constructor, or one named static method, is simpler, more discoverable and free.

The god-factory / anemic-model failure mode: once all creation (and often all rules) move into the factory, the aggregate loses its behavior and the model degenerates into a data bag maintained from outside.

Creation and reconstitution have genuinely different contracts - a new object must fail on invariant violations and receive a new identity, while a reconstituted one already has an identity and may need repair rather than rejection - so one shared method either rejects salvageable data or silently accepts invalid new objects.

Dependency direction is easy to break: a factory that loads other aggregates needs repositories, and placing it in the domain drags infrastructure inward unless those dependencies are domain-side ports.
Extra vocabulary and layers: factory is a design term, not a domain concept; too many factory classes push the model into naming that business experts do not use.

Persistence can bypass the factory: ORMs and serializers that reconstruct instances through reflection silently skip its validation, so the guarantee holds only where every construction path is actually routed through the owner.

A standalone factory with only primitive and domain-type dependencies can live in the domain layer; one that needs infrastructure services (HttpClient, external APIs) must live in infrastructure, breaking the symmetry of domain-layer creation methods.
Factory methods on aggregate roots work for most cases but can bloat the aggregate class when creation logic exceeds ~40 lines; extracting a standalone factory adds a new type to the model.
Testing factories that reach across aggregates or external services requires mocking or in-memory adapter implementations, which adds testing overhead compared to plain constructor calls.

participants.responsibility: Asks for a domain object by intent (a named creation path) and receives a complete, valid object; never selects concrete classes or assembles sub-objects itself.

The creation owner: validates inputs, coordinates assembly, enforces invariants, assigns identity and returns the product or a typed failure. May be a static method on the product, a standalone factory object, or a registry of creators. The factory interface belongs in the domain layer; the reconstitution implementation may live in infrastructure.

The domain object being created (aggregate root, entity or value object). Keeps its raw construction path private to the factory so no other code can produce an unvalidated instance, and owns its behavior after birth.

One named entry point per input shape - for example from_cart for fresh creation and reconstitute for persisted state - with the validation and identity rules that belong to that path. Creation paths throw or return a failure on invariant violation; reconstitution paths repair structural defects rather than reject.
Supplied to the factory as domain-side port abstractions when creation depends on other aggregates or external state; consulted before the product is returned, never after.
For reconstitution: loads the raw representation, delegates assembly to the factory, and owns the middle and the end of the object's lifecycle, while the factory owns its beginning.

A specialized factory, often implemented as a standalone class in infrastructure, that rebuilds an aggregate from a persisted representation. It bypasses business-precondition checks and focuses on structural integrity and identity preservation.

use_cases: Creating an aggregate from a command or DTO: Order.from_cart(cart, now) validates items, prices and minimums, assigns the order id and returns a fully valid Order.

Reconstituting an aggregate from a persistence row or document inside a repository, where the identity already exists and validation focuses on structural integrity rather than business preconditions.
Translating an external system payload (payment-gateway webhook, ERP export, CSV import) into domain objects; the factory is the anti-corruption seam that keeps the wire format out of the model.
Creating a polymorphic product family (payment methods, policy types, shipment kinds) where the client codes against the interface and the factory selects and validates the concrete type.
Cross-aggregate creation whose preconditions depend on other aggregates or policies - an Invoice needs the Order, the Customer and the current TaxPolicy - with the factory handed the ports it needs.
Centralizing identity policy (UUID, sequence, deterministic natural key) instead of repeating it in every caller.

Aggregate-root creation method: ShoppingCart.createOrder() where the cart holds the preconditions (cart must not already have an order) and produces the new Order aggregate, keeping creation in the ubiquitous language.

Deterministic identity from natural key: a factory that computes an OrderId from (customerId, orderNumber) rather than generating a random UUID, ensuring the same inputs always yield the same identity.

CQRS command handling: a command handler validates the command, calls a factory method on the aggregate root, and persists the result - the factory is the seam between the command model and the domain model.

Event-sourced aggregate reconstitution: the aggregate is reconstructed by replaying events; the factory method on the aggregate is used by the event-sourced repository to create the initial blank instance before event application.

Protean (Python DDD framework): aggregate creation lives as @classmethods on the aggregate itself - named construction paths like from_cart or from_subscription_renewal that validate inputs and emit events - with standalone factory classes reserved for external-data translation, exactly the factory-method-first progression this pattern prescribes.

SeedStack business framework (Java): the domain layer declares a Factory

interface per product and extends BaseFactory, whose protected constructors are documented as 'creates a base domain factory' - production is either resolved reflectively against the produced class or bound explicitly, keeping the creation contract on the domain side.

Apex Enterprise Patterns (fflib-apex-common, Salesforce): fflib_Application.DomainFactory is a registry mapping SObjectType to domain-constructor types; Application.Domain.newInstance(records or ids) looks up the registered Constructor, throws when no constructor is bound to the type, and supports setMock overrides so domain creation is testable without org data.
avoid_when: Creation is trivial, field-for-field from already-typed inputs: use the constructor directly, or one named static method; a separate creation owner adds nothing.
Exactly one creation path exists and a single named constructor or static factory method on the object expresses it; that method is the factory.
The ORM or serializer already owns reconstitution and the object has no creation-time invariants beyond column types: do not add a second, competing creation path.
Creation is genuinely a domain operation belonging to another aggregate or value (Customer.placeOrder): model it there instead of extracting a factory that strips behavior out of the model.

The only way to check a precondition is to lock a whole table or query across aggregate boundaries: reconsider the consistency boundary first; a store constraint or a different aggregate split is the simpler owner.
The aggregate root would need infrastructure service dependencies injected into its constructor just to support factory methods: instead expose a standalone factory that receives the ports it needs.

The factory would need to orchestrate operations beyond creation (send emails, publish events, update analytics): keep the factory focused on creation; let application services handle post-creation orchestration.
anti_patterns: Constructor-wrapper factory: a create method whose body is a single constructor call, adding indirection with nothing hidden.
God factory: one factory per layer that knows every aggregate, while the aggregates themselves become anemic data holders.
Leaky product: the factory returns a concrete class (or object/any/dynamic) so clients must downcast, or leaves the constructor public so callers bypass it.
Validation after construction: the object is built first and checked afterwards, so invalid instances are observable in between.
One method for both creation and reconstitution, either silently relaxing the new-object invariant checks or rejecting data that a reconstitution path must repair.
Factory-for-everything: applying factories to trivial value objects and simple entities, adding unnecessary indirection.
Anemic aggregate with factory-only behavior: all domain logic migrates to the factory, leaving the aggregate as a data bag.
Infrastructure-in-domain factory: a domain-layer factory that directly imports infrastructure namespaces (ORM packages, HTTP clients) to perform creation.

ORM-as-factory bypass: allowing Hibernate, Entity Framework, or SQLAlchemy to hydrate entities via reflection, skipping the domain factory entirely and circumventing invariant enforcement on reconstitution.
design_principles: Information hiding: only the creation owner knows assembly order, intermediate invalid states and the concrete classes involved.
Single responsibility: creation is a responsibility of its own, and one factory per aggregate keeps exactly one owner of the creation path.
Design by contract and fail fast: preconditions and postconditions are checked at construction, so invariants hold from birth.
Dependency inversion and layering: the domain declares creation in domain terms, while reconstitution implementations live outside the model and depend inward.
Open/closed: new creation paths arrive as new named methods or registered creators, not as edits to every call site.
Ubiquitous language: creation methods are named after domain paths, not after technical steps.
Interface segregation for factory dependencies: inject only the domain-side port abstractions collaborators need, never the full repository or infrastructure service.
Reconstitution distinct from creation: these are separate entry points with different identity and validation contracts; they must not be conflated into one method.
Factory is not a service: the factory should create and validate; post-creation orchestration (event publishing, email, analytics) belongs in application services.
best_practices: Start with a factory method on the aggregate root (classmethod in Python, static factory method in Java/C#, factory method on aggregate in TypeScript); extract a standalone factory only when it needs repositories or services, translates external data, or has grown too large to sit on the object.

Follow the creation progression: inline construction (trivial) → classmethod/static factory method (multiple creation paths, moderate complexity) → standalone factory class (repository access, external data, large logic). Start simple; extract when justified.
Keep the product's constructor private to the factory and return only complete objects; one factory per aggregate.
Keep creation and reconstitution as separate entry points with their own validation and identity rules; never conflate them into one method.
Return failures as values (Result/Either/Option in languages that support them, typed error codes in others) where the language idiomatically favors it, and never return a partially built object.
Name each creation path in the domain language (from_cart, open_business, reconstitute, as_replacement) and avoid generic create/build/make names.
Inject collaborators as domain-side ports (repository interfaces, policy interfaces) and keep the factory stateless where possible; creator registries must be immutable or thread-safe.

Place the factory interface in the domain layer; place the reconstitution implementation in infrastructure when it depends on persistence-format knowledge. Creation factory implementations that need only primitives and domain objects can stay in the domain layer.
Use aggregate-root factory methods (ShoppingCart.createOrder) when creation preconditions belong to another aggregate; this keeps creation in the ubiquitous language.
Round-trip test the pair: reconstitute(create(x)) must reproduce the same state, and every construction path needs a test in isolation from persistence.
Do not inject infrastructure services (HttpClient, EntityManager, FileSystem) directly into a domain-layer factory; expose a domain-side port interface instead and implement it in infrastructure.
For polymorphic product families, use a factory registry (abstract factory) keyed by type code or discriminator, with the registry itself living in the domain layer.

When using an ORM, provide a private or protected parameterless constructor solely for the ORM's reflection-based hydration; keep all other constructors private to the factory and validate after ORM hydration if needed.
In CQRS systems, the command handler is the natural client of the factory; the factory is the seam between the command model (DTOs, raw inputs) and the domain model.

For event-sourced aggregates, the aggregate's factory method (or constructor) is used by the repository to create the blank instance before replay; the method must not emit domain events during replay, only during live creation.
sources: Evans, E., Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Chapter 6, The Life Cycle of a Domain Object, section FACTORIES (pp. 98-106).
